desc:
People stand in a line and heights[i] is the height of person i. For each person i, find the closest person who is strictly taller, looking in both directions. Closeness is measured by index distance |i - j|.

Return an array answer where answer[i] is the index of that person. If a taller person at the same distance exists on both sides, choose the one on the left (smaller index). If nobody is taller, answer[i] = -1.

Example: heights = [3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 2] gives [2, 0, 4, 2, -1, 4]. Person 1 (height 1) has taller people at distance 1 on both sides (index 0 and 2), so the left one, 0, wins.
hints: For each person the closest taller person on the left and the closest taller person on the right are independent questions. Solve each one first.

The nearest strictly greater element to the left (and to the right) is the classic monotonic-stack query: keep a stack of indices with non-increasing heights and pop everything not taller than the current person.
Run the stack once left to right for the left candidates and once right to left for the right candidates. Then per person compare the two distances, preferring the left one on a tie.
editorial: The overall closest taller person is whichever of the two one-sided candidates is nearer. So compute L[i], the nearest index to the left with a strictly greater height, and R[i], the nearest index to the right with a strictly greater height. Each is an O(n) monotonic-stack sweep: process indices in order, pop while the stack top is not taller than the current height, and the remaining top is the nearest taller person; then push the current index.

Finally combine: if only one side has a candidate, take it; if both exist, take L[i] when i - L[i] ≤ R[i] - i and R[i] otherwise, which implements the left-first tie rule. If neither exists the answer is -1. Total O(n) time and O(n) space.
